utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. We'll continue this afternoon with Mr. Moran.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's Mr. Karabdic who has the next witness. But while I am on my feet, I want to express my personal thanks for accommodating me for the meeting with President McDonald. It solved some problems, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, please, my name is Niemann. I appear with my colleague, Ms. McHenry, and Mr. Huber for the Prosecution, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Appearances for the Defence please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, my name is Edina Residovic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. Along with me, Mr. Zejnil Delalic is defended by Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Tomislav Kuzmanovic along with Niko Djuric on behalf of defendant, Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour, my name is Salih Karabdic. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me, Mr. Hazim Delic is defended by Mr. Thomas Moran, attorney from Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I am Cynthia McMurrey and I defend Esad Landzo along with co-counsel counsel, Ms. Nancy Boler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you, very much. You may now swear the witness please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did you rest from your trip?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: My name is Salih Karabdic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic and I will put a number of questions to you. I would like to ask you to state your name to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: My name is Adem Omerkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: In front of this same chamber of this Tribunal you testified on the 31st of October, 1997. Since that time, have there been any changes in your personal data?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Generally speaking, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Have there been any changes at all?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: As far as the department where I work, I don't think so. It is okay. It is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you today still work as the Chief of the Archives Department of the Army of the Federation?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Are these the same duties that you talked about and you described before this Trial Chamber on the 31st of October, 1997?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Is there in your archive a certain procedure for gathering and keeping the documents that are kept in the Archive?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. We still have a temporary rules of procedure for gathering and working with the data which we gathered during the aggression on our country. And this was signed by General Delic. And I mentioned this during the last testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do the units of the army of B and H, that is to say the Federation Army, oblige to send all their records to this archive?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they do. But I would like to state once again that there was a fire at the building of the archives and in the meantime we were in an interim facility, not in our main facility. And right now we are in a very narrow facility where the working conditions are not very good. But, in the future, we hope to solve this. With regard to this, we have gathered the documentation, but because of these conditions, we had to interrupt our activities which have to do with gathering of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: From what I understand, you have already collected a lot of information, what happened to the other records that you did not collect? What happened to this and where is this?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: The majority of the material which was -- which was -- which was -- which we should have gathered during the aggression, but we did not, was kept in the corps, in the army and some other parts of this material because of the war or because of inadequate behaviour of certain individuals was destroyed. But I do know that certain documents we cannot gather, we cannot collect, even though we are working on this and we are working very hard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, in this archive, is there also an archive of the former fourth corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, whichever was handed over to us in the normal procedure. Yes, we think that this material, that these records are with us. But I don't think that all the materials are with us. We do know that all the records have not been handed over to us. I don't know why they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the general of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did this commander issue an order to you to establish if there are any documents in your archive and did the commander do this at the request of the Defence of Mr. Hazim Delic and Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. The established procedure of our work is such that we fulfil every order of General Delic that he gives to us on a regular basis and that means that also includes all the demands of the Hague Tribunal. All the demands by the Hague Tribunal were also sent along with the requests of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: What did you do when this request came to you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: With regard to our conditions, since only myself and three other women are working on these issues now, we have done our utmost to find the requested documents. And I think that we did manage to collect the key documents. And we tried to do our best, what we could after the request of General Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did you find all the documents that were requested?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: No, we did not find all the documents. Here I have 55 copies of originals that are in our archive and 10 copies of copies which do not exist in the archive. So we have 10 copies of already made copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Then I would like to ask some more questions about your activities. When you establish whether a document is authentic or not, what characteristics of documents do you base your decisions about their authenticity upon?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I already said this last time. The key things are the seal, which can be distinguished by the colour. It's a blue and a red seal with a fleur-de-lys sign and a checker board. And then there are also signatures and we recognise a lot of signatures immediately. And then the way the document is set out, then the number and the date and also visually we can recognise some documents immediately without these key characteristics for their recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did you look for these characteristics when you were determining the authenticity of these documents that was requested from you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. That is the way we always work with all documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Does the Federation Army rely upon the documents that are kept in your archives since they are the original documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, if there's a demand for certain documents, then these documents are taken as the original ones. And if it happens that we do not have an original, but we do have a copy, then we do try to search and find the document. And then through these people that come to see us, we try to get at the document, at the original of the document. So for our army these, these documents are absolutely truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: With regard to the request of the Defence of Mr. Delic and Delalic, can you tell us how many documents you found?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: The same thing as I said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: We found 55 originals and they are in the archives and 10 of those and 10 other ones, which were not originals, but they ask if people are still mentioned in our records.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Did you inform the Defence about your findings?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did inform the Defence. And I sent the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I have the original. And this is for the Trial Chamber and these are the originals.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May the Prosecution have a copy, please. I know we got something yesterday, but what we got wasn't fully translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Document D-102/3 to 109/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us whether this letter, whether this letter with which you informed the Defence also contained a list of documents that you found?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the list that you made?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, and there's my signature here at the very end. Yes, that's that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: I move to admit this as evidence for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any objections to the...

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I really don't know. What documents are these?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: There's a list there. Now I will give you the documents themselves. These are documents which already were handed in together with the findings of a military expert, expert witness. If I could ask for the usher to come. If the usher could come again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: May we have a copy too, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: --- (Kindly be advised microphone is not activated)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Many of these documents are already evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am not positive and I could be wrong on this, but as I recall, most of them were admitted solely for the purpose of showing the basis for an expert's decision. And now they're being offered for the truth of the matter asserted therein, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For example, appointment opposite Delalic as coordinator.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in determining our position as to what we object to or what we would not, we wonder if Defence counsel could assist us in how these documents are relevant to Mr. Delic's case? We can certainly see how some of them might be relevant to Mr. Delalic's case, but just in case we're missing something, maybe Mr. Karabdic could explain how they're relevant to Mr. Delic's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: The Defence of Mr. Delic and Delalic together have engaged the expert witness and asked for him and the expert witness, by the request of both Defences, has given his testimony here. Delic wants to have -- wants to see that all the facts that were stated in the expert witness testimony to be identified and confirmed because Delic's responsibilities are also connected and depends on this. Delic has been charged with all counts of the indictment and he has been charged with nothing less than the charges that Delalic has been charged with. And, therefore, he has to show his innocence with regard to the entire indictment and to refute all the counts of the indictment and that is his right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may help a little here. Do I have your permission?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: If the Prosecution is not satisfied with this submission, then it might help the process. Are you satisfied with the explanation?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you. We are not going to object on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, they are not following up the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the documents have been placed in succession according to the list we received in this letter. And all the documents have been submitted to you here. May I address the witness, please? Sir --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I just wonder if it might help expedite things, if the Prosecution states to begin with, that there's only one in terms of this witness testifying, the copies or the original of these documents do exist in his archives, we're not going to object to that. And we don't think it's necessary to go through each document one by one. There's only one document which we would object to and that is the document No. -- Document No. 2 in terms of the copies he found. So, in other words, an after the first 55 documents, there are some documents of which he said that were copies. Document No. 2 is a document created in 1996 by an army officer at the request Ms. Residovic. And Your Honours have already found on several occasions that that document is not admissible. And so with request to this witness' testimony, that would be the only document we're objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That document from his evidence are not documents which are original to his archive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes. And we are not going to -- we are not objecting on the basis that they are copies. If the witness says there are copies in his archives, we agree that they can be admitted for the purpose of establishing that there are copies in his archives. Our objection is that this document is entirely irrelevant and objectionable, since it's something that was created just for the defence of Mr. Delalic, at Ms. Residovic's request. It is not a contemporaneous document. And on several occasions previously Your Honours have already found that this document may not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. In connection with --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour, may I answer to the Prosecution? Mr. Omerkic stated that in the archives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina there is only -- there are copies of this document, an original copy, which they consider to be the true copy. The question of content, that is another matter altogether, but this document exists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was quite clear as to the source of those documents. The first 55 authentic to him, original to his archives. The subsequent 10 are those which he found copies from elsewhere. And this is one of those which is being objected to as not authentic, as having been created much later after the event, on the request of counsel. Now, I don't know your argument against the objection, but he could not even authenticate that one, because it is, in the first place, not his document, and then, in the second place, it was not anything authentic, as far as he is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: He said that these were not originals, but were copies. However, he insisted that these copies are -- were found in the archives of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that they are used as documents, as originals, which don't exist. But he insists and stresses that these are copies. Your Honour, can I understand this, that the Prosecution has nothing against the -- doesn't object authenticity, and that except the document number 2, which you object to, that to the others you do not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the position. I think they said it already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Mr. Omerkic, please find that document number 2, the copy number 2, which has been mentioned by Madam Holmes (Phon). Tell us, where has it been kept and what do you know about it? Please, switch on the ELMO. Could the usher switch on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Well, of all these documents that I have observed, this is documents in 1992. This document we are speaking to is from 1996, and they are not the originals, as I said, with the seal. This is one out of the 10 photocopies which I have mentioned, while the rest are -- 55 are originals. And only this refers to the intervention of somebody signed by General Delic for approval for something for Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: So we have the signature, as you can see on this copy. Is it the signature of Mr. Delic?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: And the seal, is it the seal which is generally used?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: But I emphasise it is a photocopy of a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: We still haven't understood the point. It is a photocopy of a photocopy. It was not any document which is authentic to him, and he cannot certify it as such. This is what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: You said that you recognised the signature of Commander Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is your witness who you have brought to authenticate documents, and he said things which --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: We propose that also this document be submitted as evidence, evidence authenticity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You propose it, but it's not acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. All the remaining -- Your Honour, I request that all the remaining documents be submitted and accepted as evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we do, since that was the only one objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: That is all, Your Honour. And I thank you. Thank you, sir, for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the Prosecution is going to have just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Any questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have only two questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in view of the facts that you've confirmed the existence of certain photocopies in your archives, can you tell us, are the photocopies of certain documents in the archives of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, do these photocopies exist from the beginning, when the original documents were drafted?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Well, what is significant for me is that all documents we receive, which are handed into us, when they -- we receive a list, a list with the registered documents, when we check that, we see in the list what are the originals, but under certain numbers you have also photocopies, and we accept this as something which is invaluable to us. Later on, we will be trying to find the original, but we accept the photocopy in order to be -- help us in finding the original. I cannot say where the original is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as you have answered my colleague, as long as you don't have the -- find the original, you and the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina take this copy in your archive and you rely on it, in view of all the important characteristics it has, and you consider it an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: In our Army, yes. Although, I have no responsibility in connection with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was a satisfactory answer. Please give me short answers, because you have explained to my colleague the methods of your work, you mentioned that, described that also the last time. Sir, do you know that individual organs, bodies, also army bodies, submit -- ask and issue original documents to those who request it? You have, for example, sent original documents to me and Mr. Karabdic. And I ask you, is it a custom, is it usual to send out original documents, while the bodies retain a copy of the original document which has been issued?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: The rule is that this military procedure goes from the -- the request is made through the -- via the ministry, the command, and then Commander Delic, with his signature, orders me and gives me a command, what to do. We, even if we issue a photocopy, we have to -- it must be given back to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I believe you have not understood me properly. You have answered how you issue a document from the archives. I am not asking you that. We are going back to the document we have been recently discussing. If I had asked Commander Delic to inform me about a fact, do you know that the usual habitual, that they will send me the original document while they will retain a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: We do not issue originals. We send out copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't understand you. I have received originals. I won't discuss this. I have received originals -- I have received the original of the letter.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the original letter which I have signed, but the documents in the archive, as a rule, are not issued, but the letter I have sent you, it is a list -- contains a list of the documents of the photocopies and photocopies of photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, is it possible that General Delic, answering my letter and my request, also, as you have sent me a letter, is it possible that he sent me an original document, an original document which you have in your archive as a copy? Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Well, you are trying to mix me up, to confuse me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No. Don't answer.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I don't give originals to anyone. The letter I have sent to the Tribunal is an original letter with my signature. I don't know what you wanted

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is not a relevant question. This document was as a relevant document. And the Court and the Tribunal, I thank you very much for my endeavour in trying to help us. And I have no more questions for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think he is unable to issue it because he hasn't in his archives the original copies. What he has are photocopies, so he cannot satisfy photocopies as authentic. This is their rule. If he had the original copies with him in the archives. These originals do not exist in his archives. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. He just confirmed that fact you have presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Mucic has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Esad Landzo has no questions of this witness either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Any questions for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Yes, very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omerkic. How are you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Hello. And how are you, madam?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Fine, thank you. Sir, when you have documents in your archives, can you tell from what source the document came from; in other words, who gave it to your archives, whether or not it's the fourth corps or the supreme command or some other unit? Can you tell that or not with your documents?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: No, from the document you cannot see. But you have the minutes on the submission of the documents of their handing them in. And it does happen that from the chiefs of staff, from the supreme command, or from the corps, we receive their archives, they hand in the material, archive material. On that occasion we said the minute, we write it down, that the archives -- this is a report where the right archives have been handed in. So on the basis, if one read the acts, one could -- the documents, one could see where they came from, their source.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: So, in other words, you can't tell from looking at a document who gave it to the archives, but with enough time you could reconstruct who gave it to the archives, by looking at other minutes and such things? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the report on the handing them in. But we could reconstruct it also differently in other ways.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, with respect to the 102 documents that you were asked to find and could not locate, either originals or copies in your archives, do you have a list of those documents with you?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I have a list of documents that I have submitted here, 55 originals, they are photocopies, and a list of 10 photocopies of photocopies

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Maybe if I could just ask if Defence Counsel would --

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I made that list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If Defence Counsel, Mr. Karabdic, could provide me a list after this witness's testimony of the documents that were not able to be located, I think that would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You really need them?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: I think it may help us in the future. It may be relevant. I don't want to interrupt this witness's testimony now. But it might be relevant, and it might also save time in the future, rather than us asking him to look for documents that he's already looked for and determined were -- could not be found in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: We have the request of the authentication of documents which have been submitted in addition to the expert witness of the military area. The other documents -- we have in that report the documents which could not be found, and the listing.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Sir, I just have one question about a particular document that you found, and it's number -- it's again a document that you found a copy of, not the original. And it's document number 8 in your letter. And it's a report from 6th -- I'm sorry, 6th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Sixth of December. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Now, could you just find your copy of that for me.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I have my photocopy. I have photocopied it, the documents for myself prior to coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And that document refers to certain attachments which are integral parts of the report. Can you tell me now, are you in a position to tell me whether or not the copy in your archives has all the attachments or not?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Mainly, yes. In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Although, one of the documents with many attachments, I took just the first page and the last page with the seal, but in our register we have the report and as well as all the attachments.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And would you agree, when you go back you can look and see whether or not your archives has all the attachments, in particular to this particular document that I am referring to, this 6th of December report? Could you do that for me, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: But you have to turn to our General, and it will be my pleasure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And, in fact, it's correct that very recently you were asked to find, locate some other documents in your archives, but you did not have sufficient time and have indicated you will do that after the appropriate steps have been taken and you have time to look for additional documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I know. I said everything that I had received the orders, I will do. And I am at your disposal to the maximum, of course. But I have to receive the order, which I then execute. I don't know what you really mean by that. Do you want to say that I didn't do what I promised I would do?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Absolutely not, sir. I did not mean to suggest that for one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You don't have to be angry. You don't have to be angry.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: I am not angry. The Prosecutor is a distinguished lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: And, in fact, sir, I will represent to you that with respect to any additional request we have, I will try to work with Defence Counsel to see if we can agree that the documents can be admitted without making you come back again. And thank you, sir, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your appearance. Okay. You are discharged now.

utterances.speaker: ADEM OMERKIC.
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Our next witness will be Mr. Demic. Your Honour, while he is being brought in, I was going through some documents and there was something I forgot to do back in February, and I would like to do it now. As the court will recall, when Mr. Gow was on the stand, I showed him several documents from the Security Council. And by just pure forgetfulness on my part I forgot to introduce D16/3, which is a letter from the Security Council president; 17/3, which is a letter from the permanent representative of Canada to the president of the Security Council; B18/3, which is a letter of the -- another letter from the permanent representative of Canada; and D19/3, which is a letter from the deputy permanent representative of the United States to the president, Security Council. Just so the record would be complete, I move to introduce those at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let him take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Take your seat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, those documents, are they admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I have not even seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, they are in the record. We'll do it at another time that may be more convenient to the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Can't we take judicial notice of those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you can. I don't think there is any reason to introduce them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What's the position of the Prosecutor, with regard to resolution of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: My position has been very clear, public documents, documents which establish facts of those nature can be taken judicial notice of, and you don't have to tender them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I think the court is correct. I just had introduced some others and tendered them and they were admitted into evidence, and I was going through the exhibit list and there was great big boldface "not tendered," and I thought that I ought to be consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can send them onto the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge, that's all I need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Demic.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My name is Tom Moran and, if you will give me a second, I am hearing Bosnian. There we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I thought you must have learnt Bosnian by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am here to tell you that most of the Bosnians have learned more English than I have Bosnian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Ms. McMurrey is very good at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, she spent more time in Konjic than I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Demic would you please introduce yourself to the Trial Chamber. Tell us how you are employed.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Bajram Demic. I was born on the 9th of April, 1959 in Rozaje. I work at the radio television of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Are you a married man, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And do you have any children?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I'm a father of five -- four.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's three more than I have, and I hope that you have fewer headaches than I do. Sir, how long have you been employed by the television -- radio television of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I reported on my duty in 1992 on the 9th of May for the first time in the radio television of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: The radio of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you work for any other television stations or newspapers prior to going to work for the radio of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I worked in Vecernji List, which is a daily newspaper from Zagreb. I was a correspondent of Monitor, which is an independent weekly from Titograd from Montenegro, and I worked for other independent newspapers. And I also worked for HTV nine months before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, what is HTV?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: It's a Croatian radio television. Now they call it HRT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, at some point during the summer of 1992, were you -- did you see a report on television from Pale concerning some allegations of mistreatment of Serbs held in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, I heard about this report, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, basically, what was the report? What did it say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That's hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, well, it's going to show the motive for why he did the events that he's going to be the personal witness for. And if the Court likes, I'll withdraw the question and just say based on that, did you do something? I thought that the Trial Chamber might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: From what he heard, may have heard from someone else. And though --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I say something now? There seems to be a misunderstanding. When I said that I heard about it, I heard it in the radio, I didn't see it on television. That means I heard it in radio Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, basically, and just very short, what was that report about? In no great detail, just in general.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: In this report, it was stated that the detainees in Celebici are being kept hungry and that they live in abnormal conditions and other things similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And based on that report, did you and a colleague do anything?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, knowing from before, about the propaganda, the mentioned station from Pale, we did not feel any special need to deny this. However, as journalists, we had this idea that we might, maybe, take a look at this prison that was being mentioned to make a report, a story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, by the way, who was your colleague?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: My colleague, her name was Jadranka Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did you and your colleague go to the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: First we talked about doing this, but we didn't have any particular plan or time to go there. And since there was not enough gas at the time, we had a car. I don't know if this is important or not, which was of the make of Wartburg, which is an East German make. And on this summer day, we bought some gas in Jablanica because it could be bought there. And on our return, since we had a camera on our backseat, we decided to try our luck and to see whether we can make this story. And even if we don't manage to make one, we would not have been too disappointed. Earlier we had heard that it wasn't really a big problem to enter this camp and that other international organisations could enter this camp and that it was not a big deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did you call ahead to the camp or to anyone else to give any advance notice of your visit or did you just decide relatively on the spur of the moment, "Let's go to the camp," and then drove directly to the camp? Or, whatever, or if it was something different, whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I think we made our decision at around Ostrozac, which is a town before Celebici. We went to the gate of this prison. I left the car because the gate was closed. And there I saw from that small house which was there, a young man. And I tried to explain to him what our intentions were and I think he was a little bit unprepared for that. He said politely that we should wait here, as if he was looking for somebody that he could consult with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, when you say the small house, if you look in front of you, there is a model. In fact, you can get up and walk around and take a look at it. And see if you can locate that small house. And on the top of it, there should be a letter. And if you'd tell us what letter it is. Like I say, you can get up and walk around over there, if you want to, whatever makes it easier for you to see.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: It was this house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The one with the "A" on top of it?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Just a second, let me have a better look. Yes, this facility here. It was the administrative building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, the one with the little A, is that the one where the guard was?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: It was a kiosk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And when the guard left, what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: That we should wait for a moment. And then at this other building, because I was waiting at that gate, I saw in front of it a man who was washing a car and the make was a Fiat. It's a very small car, I don't know if you know about it. It's made by Fiat. And this car was quite old, I remember that. And I said it was a rock car. We were joking about this car for a while. And these people talked to each other for a while. Then they came up to me. And he again said that I should wait for a while. This man was older than this young guy that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The older man, you say the young man brought an older man with him; is that what happened?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, that's what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And the older man said wait for a few more minutes? Wait here?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of that older man?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. At that moment I did not know his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Do you know him or do you see him in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: In the grey sweater.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the record can reflect, he's identified my client. What happened next, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Soon after that, we entered. We parked our car, not by the building, but on the right from the gate. I took a camera and we went towards the administrative building. I was waiting there for a while and then we talked for a while. After that, a man came out and he said his name was Pavo. And I had never seen him before that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what did Pavo tell you, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: He asked me what we wanted. We repeated what we had already said earlier. He said, you can take, film everything. And he, I think he joked that he didn't want us to make any film of him because he was not very photogenic, the camera didn't like him. And we laughed, so that the atmosphere was very relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did Pavo tell you what his job was at the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, not at that point, but we could have guessed what his job was. That he was one of the people who was kind of in charge and he gave us permission to film that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what did you and your colleague do next?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, he did not want to be present. He left to that other building. He left us outside. Some other younger people came, some soldiers. And we said that we wanted, I personally, actually, asked for it, to film Zara, who was a prisoner that I knew was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Zara who?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Because he was a guy who had a cafe in Bradina, which still exists, this facility still exists. And everybody knew --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was Zara's full name? Do you know his full name?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: The cafe was called Zara, at Zara's, and everybody called him by that name, he was the only person by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Could be, if you don't know, you don't know?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, I know him. He was a big guy. And before the war I knew him and also his brother. And just before the war, I gave his brother -- I lent a book to his brother, which is called "Knife" by Vuk Draskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said you asked to see Zara, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: One of the men said that he was somewhere around. And that he shouted loudly and they called him two or three times and then he showed up in some T-shirt and he had jeans on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, were there a lot of people wandering around inside the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, there were. When I asked to see his brother, whom I also knew, they also called him and he came behind a facility where he was doing something, cleaning something. There were some people also who were sitting below a roof because it was quite hot on that day and there was more than one person sitting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if these people were inmates or guards or do you have any way of telling? Were they wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: They were wearing civilian clothes. And there were also others. But I knew for sure that those who were cleaning the compound that they were inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, did you get a good look at these people?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I looked at them for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did they look like they had been starved or beaten?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir, after you got -- after you found your friend Zara, did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: He's not my friend. He's an acquaintance and I was friends with his brother. But he was interesting to me because I knew, and many others knew, that he was rich. And that he was in some kind, in some way a logistics person and that he was procuring weapons for the Serb population in Bradina. That was no secret. And I wanted to see how such a person would be treated who was called the duke, Vojvoda. And then I could have guessed how others were treated if I could see how the main guy was treated. That would have been some kind of a measurement, how these people were treated in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, did you talk to him? Have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, for a very short period. I asked him what he was doing there and he told me -- and I am not quite sure that he was colonel or lieutenant colonel, I am not quite sure, who was a commanding officer of the former JNA. He went to see off his family to safety by a helicopter from a heliodrome which existed in Bradina on a road in front of the former barracks. And he did not come back. And then they were seized by panic because the commander had not returned, the colonel or the lieutenant colonel. And, actually, they were supposed to attack on the 27th of May in the direction of Tarcin and Pazaric to join with the Serbs from Ilidea.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Who was this lieutenant colonel?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: He was a lieutenant colonel, an officer of the former Yugoslav National Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Mr. Mrkajic or was that somebody else?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. This officer did not go back. He left by a helicopter of the former JNA in order to bring his family to safety. And then he never returned to command this unit which was located in Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, let's focus on the camp and your time in the camp if we could. Because, frankly, the four defendants here are charged -- occurred in the camp.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: You asked me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, that's fine. When you were talking to Mr. Mrkajic, was anyone with you? Was Pavo with you or was Mr. Delic with you? Was there anyone there monitoring the conversation?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And I take it that when you say you had a conversation, you were closer than you and I are, you're just two people standing there having a conversation?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, my colleague, Jadranka Milosevic, was also there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So it was two journalists and Mr. Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And did he complain to you about being beaten or other prisoners being beaten?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did he complain to you about being starved?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. He complained more because this officer left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So he was more unhappy because someone that he thought was a friend of his, deserted from Bradina before the battle, rather than about conditions in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, he was sorry or he saw that as treason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did you film your interview with Zara?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Does that film still exist?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, I didn't ask you to bring it, did you? But you could bring it if the Prosecutor asked you or someone asked you, you could provide that film?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Did Zara mention anything to you about people being allowed to visit the camp and bring the prisoners anything?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: While we were talking, and I think this was also being taped, he said that they had visitation rights and that three times food was brought to them. I remember that my colleague, after he had said this, reacted, I would say, unprofessionally. And she said that they have a better time than the soldiers of the army in the -- on the frontlines. I think that he might not have heard very well what she said and then he asked a question about that. And she was obviously upset about this, my colleague, Milosevic. And I stopped the filming. I think that in a way I also understood what she was coming from because she knew, just as I did, that her brother in Sarajevo, in the beseeched Sarajevo, and that he basically had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, sir, while you were there, did you have occasion to talk to a man named Branko Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, we didn't ask for this man by name. But since there were some talks about starving the inmates, we asked for somebody who was distributing or cooking the food. And they said, actually they called this man and he showed up in some shirt and he made a statement and I filmed it and my colleague interviewed him, asked him what it was like, asked him about some conditions. He gave this statement and I think this statement has also been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And do you know whether he was a prisoner or whether he was a guard or a staff member?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, he was a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what did he tell you about the food?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: He said that it was mostly satisfactory. As far as I remember, he said that what is remained and not distributed is given to those people who have larger appetites. It's the so-called second helping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And was there anyone around besides you and your colleague while this part of the interview was going on? Were there any guards or staff members there?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, they were standing on the side. And some prisoners also came and guards. So they were all mixed. We, at the same time, also filmed the infirmary, the clinic, so to speak, which was there in the facility across this red, dark red building. That's facility C, building C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, while you were -- tell us about the filming at the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: They showed me where the infirmary was. It was very hot. I'd opened the door. I wasn't sure, but I think there was about 10 beds in there. And on these beds, there were patients lying. In the middle of this room, there were some -- there was a table with wheels. And on this table were some medicines and some infusion equipment, something for infusion. I greeted to them and I said that I would be filming them. They greeted me back and I started filming them. I am not a professional reporter and I was filming with the so-called schwenk, the entire room.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just one second, sir. The translation I heard was you were not a professional reporter and I am informed that what you said is you were not a professional photographer, which is it? Are you a professional reporter?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Are you a professional photographer?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Before the war, I did some work with the VHS camera. And during the war, since our cameraman was in detention in Hadzici for about two months, I, as a male person, accepted to work with the camera and that my colleague can then work as a reporter. And every expert that knows anything about filming will see that in my filming there is a zoom with a broad angle, which a professional cameraman would never do. But those were the times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So basically you were pressed into service to be a photographer because you could handle that big camera better than your colleague who was a small woman?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I am a gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you very much, sir. Sir, tell us more about the interviews with the doctors. First, do you remember the doctors names?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I remember the hefty man, his name was Relja. I don't remember the name of the other man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Did your colleague interview these people while you were filming them?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was there anyone around, any guards or any staff or any people? Was Pavo around, for instance, or Hazim, or was it just basically the four of you while you were doing this interview?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I think that on the unedited material, you will see that there was nobody except for the four of us. I am sure you will see also film, images shot at a broader angle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall what these two doctors told you during this interview?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I cannot quote, but I think that maybe I could outline the most characteristic elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sure, just do the best you can, sir.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: The first interviewee, I don't remember his name. He gave an imprecise statement. When he, when my colleague asked him, who are the people in the infirmary? He said that in addition to the people who were injured in combat, that there were also people who were imprisoned in the sports facility in Konjic, who were injured. He said it. They were injured by some kind of grenade. And I think it was quite clear of what -- he then again said, well, when Konjic was shelled and we know who shelled Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. And did the other doctor say anything to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, she asked him about the cooperation with the hospitaling of Konjic. And I think it was a very relaxed discussion. Simply because that doctor, and I don't remember his name, he insisted at the end of each question, when answering, he wanted to add always something. And we allowed that. He said that they were prisoners and that now they have been released. That they go home every day and return. And we have agreed about this segment and we then had it in, when edited, it was included. I don't know whether it was all then shown on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, and after, did you see anyone else at the camp or talk to anyone else after the camp, after you met with the doctors and Zara and Mr. Cecez?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I also met with Zara's brother, but that was before the filming. And I talked to him on the lawn, a very short talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And while you were talking to him, did he complain about being beaten or starved or abused?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You said the weather was very hot that day, were people complaining about not having water to drink or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, no, absolutely not. You could see that somebody was washing, somebody was washing a car and they were watering the lawn. They had a house --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber will rise for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: And come back at five.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I remind you, sir, that you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please take your seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: May it please the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, again. Sir, about how long in total was your visit in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: About half an hour, maybe approximately 40 minutes, but I doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: While you were there, did you have occasion to go into any of the warehouses or hangars that are around the facility there?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, nothing except the infirmary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Was that because you didn't want to, or was that because somebody told you you couldn't?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, we received and we were granted more than we expected. We found a more relaxed atmosphere than one could expect for a camp, for a prison, and we also had access to the person we asked for. I think that we satisfied the journalists' code. We asked and, to my judgement, we were asking and talking to one of the main Serbs who rebelled, then a person who was distributing food, the doctors, and the only thing that was left out, which was missing, was the side, the party under whose -- under whose command the prison was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. So nobody stopped you from going in? You could have gone anywhere you wanted to in the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Absolutely. We were standing there, we were talking to the prisoners, detainees, to the soldiers or the camp guards, who were dressed in civilian, half civilian, half uniform type of apparel. And we saw that they were joking among themselves because probably they knew each other even before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now, when you were going around the camp, did you have an escort from the guards? For instance, in this building, when you go from one place to another, you have a guard escorting you, right?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. The guard -- in the first -- we were moving around mainly in the first part of the camp where the prisoners were watering the lawn and the trees. With Zara, I talked to Zara on the lawn behind the infirmary, and we were alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, about when was this visit to the camp, roughly?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I must say, in view of all the events and the entire war, I really cannot remember exactly the date and the time, but it could be asserted on the basis of the film. It was aired on television. It's been put in archives. Or, if you want to, I know that some three, four or five days later in this camp there was people -- people were under oath, giving their oath, the new soldiers were giving the oath of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it was -- we filmed that reportage three or four days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, if I told you that that was -- that ceremony was on August the 16th, would you agree with me that, then, your visit to the camp would have had to have been sometime around August the 10th, August the 11th, August the 12th, around then?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Quite probably, but I think we could see that on the film. I have the film at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, also, after you left the camp -- well, let me back off. Did you have any contacts with any representatives of the International Committee for the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Not after that. You mean immediately after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, no, no. At any time during this period.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And what did they ask you about, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: They were interested in the Red Cross and the prisoners in the camps, and I helped them as much as I could. They told me that they have visited that camp. Once I told them of the existence of the camp, they told me they visited it. I showed them the refugees, refugees from Eastern Bosnia who lived under open skies in the Igman, on the slopes of Igman and Bjelasnica. And they visited them, they recorded, registered all of this. These refugees couldn't be sheltered in Pazaric and Tarcin, since their people, non-Serbs from Hadzic, were located there after the aggression against Hadzici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir, when you talked to the ICRC representatives, did they ask you about how you get into a camp, or did they indicate to you that they had had any problems getting into any camps?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. No, they asked -- I told you that they visited that camp even before we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Sir, back in October of 1996, do you remember talking to a representative from the Office of the Prosecutor named Sabine Manke?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I didn't know at the time that she is a Prosecutor. I thought that she was a Prosecutor of the Tribunal in The Hague. She can confirm that. I offered my cooperation. I offered her all of the filmed material. She gave me her visiting card and I gave her my telephone numbers to that visit card. I believe it said on the visiting card that she is a police inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Sir, in your statement to Ms. Manke, you told her that the visit was towards the end of June, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I am not sure that I said that. It's possible that I make a mistake, but not such a big mistake in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Sir -- so it's possible that when you talked to Ms. Manke, you could have been mistaken about the time of your visit to the camp?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I could make a mistake, but not for such a long period of time. Maybe I said July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: But you can see it on the film, the dates are printed on the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine, sir. I just wanted to let everyone know that you had -- that there was a difference in dates. When you had your interview with Ms. Manke and you gave her the written statement, did you have a lot of time to prepare for that and get your thoughts together and make -- or was it just kind of a sudden thing, while you were willing to cooperate, you didn't have time to check notes? Which was it, sir?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No, I didn't have the time. Absolutely not. I think I was working in the field as a reporter, I received the message, I went and visited two skyscrapers, which were burned down during the shelling of Sarajevo, and I think that we had this talk on the 8th or 10th floor of one of these two skyscrapers. We discussed it in a relaxed atmosphere, and she can confirm that I had no time to prepare myself. And we even joked during this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. But as you sit here today and having thought about it, the best that your memory is, is this visit to the camp was the 10th, 11th, 12th, 13th of August, not June or July; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, it would be impossible. June would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Fine. I thank you very much, Your Honour. I pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any cross-examinations?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Demic. I am Edina Residovic, and I am the Defence Counsel of Mr. Delalic. Mr. Demic, we've met before.

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes. As I began as a journalist, I knew from the media. But you didn't know me, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you. Sir, during the main examination you said you heard on the radio that they are poorly fed, namely, the Serbs imprisoned in Celebici. On the other hand, is it true that you've heard from our fighters that the conditions under which the prisoners lived are even better than those for our soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: On a number of occasions I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before I continue, Mr. Demic, with questions, which I will be addressing to you, I would only like to ask you whether it's true that your pseudonym is Zvonko Maric?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But this pseudonym, this Zvonko Maric, you used it as a war reporter from the free territories of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, even today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is why you, Mr. Demic, will not be angry if I occasionally address you as Mr. Maric?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: It's all the same to me. Even I don't know -- make the distinction any more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you have heard from Radio Srna, on the other hand you heard something from our combatants, you -- this all caused a rise of interest in you, and you wanted to confirm the facts?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that already at that time you have been convinced a number of times that from the Serb radio, and from the Serb television, certain untruths are being aired on the situation in the area where you were living at the time?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, quite a number of times. After the liberation of Gradina, for example, Radio Srna said the information was -- said -- aired that 5.000 Serbs were detained in a tunnel. I was passing by that tunnel every day, and I knew that there were no Serbs were detained there. And even more drastic, as I see it, ten young soldiers of the former JNA, who were detained in the barracks of Pazaric Krupa, Srna aired, as did Radio Belgrade, that they were hanged in Tarcin in the town square. Tarcin is a village and it has no village square. That's on the first account. Secondly, these young soldiers for a long time were sleeping in the same premises as the soldiers of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Then they were liberated and returned home to their respective homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have confirmed that we know each other. Is it also true that in June, 1996 you have told the investigator, Mrs. Kreso -- gave a statement concerning this report and the filming of the report in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that after that -- to me, as the Defence Counsel of Mr. Delalic, you gave me the original, unedited material of the reportage from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, I gave it to you, as I would to any other official person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior to the war, Mr. Demic, you did not know Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Just you got to know him by accident in Konjic, when he stopped to greet his friends and your common friends?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, that was in front of the cultural house in Konjic, and possibly somebody from the command was there, and maybe the headquarters of certain services.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You can also confirm that that was somewhere in the month of June, when you heard from your acquaintances, who were greeted by Mr. Delalic, that he worked in the area of logistics?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, during the main examination, and let's go back to the reportage in Celebici, you said that the person who introduced himself as Pavo enabled you to shoot that what you wanted to film?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes, without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were accompanied by your colleague, Jadranka Milosevic, is it true that both your colleague and you had an interest -- were interested in asserting and confirming a number of pieces of information, namely, are people starving, the detainees, are they starving, what is the treatment of the most important prisoners, and, thirdly, what was the status and the care for the sick people there? I wanted to ask, were these the main objectives of your visit there?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to ask that Madam Residovic not lead the witness. I know it's not her witness, but it was her witness originally on her witness list. If she wants to obtain the evidence from the witness now because an opportunity presents itself, I certainly don't object to that. But I do object to leading in these circumstances, because, really, it's practically no different to her actually calling the witness herself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ask him the normal questions and he will answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I err in questions, please make notice of that. I will reformulate -- rephrase the questions. But, of course, we are interested in all witnesses, including the witnesses of the --

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I am a bit embarrassed. Nobody has led me. This is -- I feel a bit offended with this remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think you didn't understand what he meant by leading questions. You did not understand that. It's not your language. It's not even your profession. We have said things which are related to how counsel should introduce questions. So listen to your counsel carefully and answer questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you want to determine what the state of feeding the prisoners in the camp of Celebici was?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Well, we wanted to determine the events, but this is also something that any journalist would want to find out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the examination in chief, Mr. Demic, you mentioned that you, without any problems, entered the barracks. Could you please tell us, at the moment when you were entering the barracks, at the moment when you were arranging what kind of things to shoot, at the moment of the actual shooting and after you had left the barracks, did you at any time in the barracks of Celebici see or meet Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. I can retake my solemn declaration on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Demic, prior to what you called a sudden decision to visit the Celebici camp, ever talk to Mr. Delalic about your wish to go to this barracks? My question is, is it -- my question is whether it is true that you have never spoken about this to Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: I have never spoken to anybody about this specifically. I mentioned the possibility of my visit to the camp to make this story, but, as I mentioned, we were assured that there would be no problems, and I would say this in front of a large number of people, and it was possible that Mr. Delic (sic) was there when we met. Maybe I mentioned it at that time too. I do not exclude that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Demic, before the interview with these doctors, did you, with them together, sit in some of the rooms of the administrative building?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, before you started your interviews with the doctors and other persons, make any arrangements, what kinds of questions you would be asking of those persons?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, after you had made the interview, go to the administrative building and sit with anybody there, and, specifically, did you take a seat there with the doctors that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: No. Absolutely not. Particularly, because it was very hot and it was much more convenient to sit not in this building, but in another building which was -- whose doors were open.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Demic, you are absolutely positive, you are absolutely certain, and you can confirm that during the entire time of your stay in the compound of the barracks, Celebici, you never met or saw Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that after you had finished your task that you had given to yourself in the barracks of Celebici, that you left for Konjic?

utterances.speaker: Bajram Demic
utterances.text: Yes. And we were very pleased about what we've done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
